plants.name: Paeonia lactiflora
plants.description: Big, ruffled, sweetly fragrant blooms open from plump buds and weigh down the stems. They put on a lavish show in cottage gardens and borders across the temperate Northern Hemisphere.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late April to early June, depending on cultivar. Late-season varieties are still in flower around June 4.
plants.location: Gardens across temperate North America and Europe. The species is native to China, Siberia and Tibet.
plants.funFact: Peonies can live for decades in the same spot, and some garden clumps outlive the people who planted them. Ants are often seen on the buds, but they aren't needed to make the flowers open.

plants.name: Protea cynaroides
plants.description: This is the largest flower in the protea family, with a bowl-shaped crown of silky pink bracts around a central cone. It blooms on the fynbos slopes of the Western Cape just as the cool, wet winter begins.
plants.bloomingSeason: Mainly winter and spring, from June to October. In the Southern Hemisphere, early June is the start of its peak.
plants.location: The fynbos of South Africa's Western Cape, including the slopes around Cape Town and Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden.
plants.funFact: The king protea is South Africa's national flower. Its thick, fire-adapted stems regrow from underground after bushfires, and its flower heads are often visited by sugarbirds and beetles.

plants.name: Banksia serrata
plants.description: A rugged coastal tree with zigzag, saw-toothed leaves. It bears chunky, candle-like flower spikes in pale green and cream, and nectar-seeking honeyeaters crowd the branches.
plants.bloomingSeason: Flowers from summer to winter, peaking in autumn, so it is still blooming in early June, the start of Australian winter.
plants.location: Coastal eastern Australia, from Queensland through New South Wales and Victoria to Tasmania.
plants.funFact: After the flowers fade, the spikes turn into woody, knobbly seed cones. These stay sealed until fire passes through, which makes the species well suited to Australian bushland.
